reported in Table S14, Table S15, and Table S17, respectively.

Having observed these predictive outcomes, we confirmed that our discovered Reff played a critical role in revealing a relatively substantial difference in GM density. Thus, this piece of evidence assisted in exploiting Reff because of its promise to distinguish most class-discriminative regions. We quantitatively compared our method with several Deep Learning (DL) baselines, including CNN-based [17], [47] (ResNet18 [47], ResAttNet [17]) and Transformer-based [48], [49], [50] methods (ViT [48], M3T [49], and DSTANet [50]). ResNet18 is a representative image classifier known for superior performance. ResAttNet combines ResNet with self-attention modules. ViT treats image patches as sequential input, while M3T synergically models CNN and Transformer architectures, exploiting 2D views from 3D MRIs. DSTANet utilizes a Transformer with diffusion kernel attention, taking brain ROIs as input, similar to our LiCoL. Results from all DL baselines were distilled with cGMs for a fair assessment, and cGM augmentation notably improved performance across all baselines. Interestingly, sequential modeling methods generally performed better, while ViT showed relatively lower performance, potentially due to a lack of training samples.

It is noteworthy that LiCoL, despite being a lightweight classifier, achieved performance on par with DL baselines in binary scenarios and state-of-the-art performance in the multi-class scenario. DL models, built on complex non-linear networks with numerous parameters, sacrifice interpretability for high classification performance. Conversely, LiCoL was designed with linearity to ensure interpretable internal representations, similar to conventional ML models. This allows for straightforward understanding of classification decisions without additional tools. We further investigated the variability in (m)AUC performance using common or additive Reff discrepant ROIs (R′eff) and Rstat discrepant ROIs (R′stat). To evaluate the validity of these ROIs, we categorized them into: (i) baseline (Reff and Rstat), (ii) intersection (Reff ∩ Rstat), and (iii) union (Reff ∪ R′stat or Rstat ∪ R′eff). We re-trained LiCoL with each ROI combination.

As revealed in Table 3, the best predictive performance was achieved using the baseline Reff. Using intersection and union derived from Reff showed a slight decreasing tendency in several scenarios, suggesting R′stat does not significantly contribute to performance improvement despite statistical significance. However, the union with Rstat exhibited an average (m)AUC performance improvement (ADNI: 1.49%↑ and GARD: 1.11%↑) over baseline. This indicates that utilizing discrepant ROIs R′eff enhanced predictive scores by reflecting distinct differential regions resulting from disease progression. Thus, R′eff could be elucidated as potential biomarkers not apparent in statistical tests but substantial in disease-related variations. Comprehensive results revealed two instances of R′eff and intersection ROIs across all scenarios of both ADNI and GARD. The intersection ROIs included regions like L.PreCG, L/R.SFG, L/R.MFG, and others known as prevalent AD-related landmarks.

As R′eff, L.PFCventmed was observed across all scenarios for ADNI, and the CN vs. MCI and CN vs. MCI vs. AD scenarios for GARD, while R.PFCventmed was discovered within the CN vs. MCI and CN vs. MCI vs. AD scenarios for both ADNI and GARD. Further analysis in ADNI revealed L.MCC, L.MOG, R.IPG, L.SMG, L/R.IFGoperc, and R.PCUN as R′eff in the CN vs. MCI and CN vs. MCI vs. AD scenarios, whereas L.ACCpre was discovered in all scenarios. On GARD, L.PCUN was found in the CN vs. MCI and CN vs. MCI vs. AD scenarios. Visualizing common and discrepant ROIs on ADNI and GARD using 3D-volume mapping (Fig. S4) facilitated intuitive understanding. We devised LiCoL by revoking incomprehensible non-linearities, embracing a linear function for intuitive interpretation. We present the mathematical development of LiCoL as a linear function and analyze the input-dependent representation of CAˆxs (AD-relatedness index) to reveal the contribution of each ROI for patient-specific prediction.

We used the counterfactual-guided attention map CA as the region-wise AD-related importance to support the LiCoL decision. Fig. 5 illustrates the region-wise AD-relatedness indices over groups and individual patients in each scenario on ADNI and GARD. Group-wise investigation showed that AD-effect ROIs for CN vs. AD were closely related to AD prediction, as morphological differences were immense. Meanwhile, the AD-relatedness index for individual patients varied despite being guided by coherent AD-effect ROIs Reff, indicating LiCoL considered regional differences in GM density and reflected individual characteristics. ROIs like L/R.HIP, L/R.STG, L/R.IFGoperc, and L.PreCG exhibited especially high AD-relatedness indices in all scenarios. The HIP, a prominent region showing atrophy in AD, is an index of AD neuropathology and an early marker. The temporal region (STG) is known for structural variations in AD-manifested brains.

Notably, R.INS and L/R.PCUN were not essential ROIs for CN prediction but became crucial for diagnosing MCI or AD patients. L.SMA markedly contributed to diagnosing MCI, and R.IPG was significant in AD. Additionally, L/R.SFG and L/R.MFG, located in the frontal area, are associated with AD. Based on in-depth analyses via LiCoL’s transparency, we validated that the DL model (CMG) well-generated the target properties of which regions in the brain to change the classifier’s prediction as the brain disease progressed. AD-relatedness indices could provide neuroscientific insights for disease stratification and understanding of individual symptoms, facilitating more specified diagnostic criteria for personalized inspection. We further explored whether cGM augmentation could overcome issues encountered in the medical field, such as accurate prevalence estimates of dementia by age. Table 4 examines precision and recall according to the number of samples for each age group in the MCI vs. AD scenario, demonstrating alleviation of spurious correlations by using cGM.

us risk factors w.r.t AD manifestation, with the percentage of the population who have AD increasing dramatically with age. However, although 3% of people aged 65 ∼74, 17% of people aged 75 ∼84, and 32% of people aged 85 or older have been diagnosed as AD patients [56], it is important to note that AD is not a normal part of aging [57], and older age alone is not considered a sufficient factor to cause AD. Various medical studies [58], [59] call this phenomenon spurious correlation, which occurs when two factors appear to be correlated to each other, but in fact are not [60]. Furthermore, few AD cases are identified when the patient’s age is younger than 65 years, and further data on the prevalence of brain disease are scarce. Hence, samples of a specific age or clinical stage are lacking, which leads to an undesirable bias. We thus exploited the cGMs as augmented samples to alleviate these practical issues.

For this purpose, we used the set of Rstat and Reff as the classifier’s input (use our LiCoL) to demonstrate the fidelity of cGM augmentation by showing that the performance shifts, which depend on whether augmented data are included in the training. As reported in Table 4, the precision of the trained LiCoL that used Rstat was found to be relatively lower in young AD (i.e., aged 60 ∼70) on ADNI as well as elderly MCI (i.e., aged 80 ∼90) on GARD. Furthermore, unlike in the ADNI, a lack of samples appeared in the 80 ∼90 age range in GARD, and this age range exhibited the lowest precision. In this light, we can assume that precision degradation was derived due to the undesirable spurious correlation. However, when statistical ROIs were constructed along with cGM (i.e., Rstat w/ cGM), the performance with augmentation was noticeably improved across all age ranges.

Particularly, it should be noted that the precision for the aged 80 ∼90 on GARD dramatically increased by +19.19%. Through these results, we argued that the auxiliary cGMs of a patient at different clinical stages provided informative features, so that LiCoL could learn how to correctly distinguish the discriminative characteristics of each clinical stage, depending on the age range. Thus, we suggest distilling cGMs can be beneficial for mitigating the data-hungry problem in practical settings and promising alternatives for solving spurious correlations.
4
DISCUSSION
The goal of GM density manipulation in this study is to normalize the individual brain image so that it aligns to a consistent anatomical space to account for personal variability. From this perspective, GM density maps might induce the disappearance of individual-specific shape information and minor structural distortions due to mapping into the shared template during the manipulation.

However, contrary to these concerns, the variations in density values across the GM density maps after registration still represent crucial information. GM density maps take into account the fact that the size and shape of brains can vary considerably among individuals during the registration process; hence GM density values within these maps present GM volume so that it enables us to facilitate meaningful comparisons by focusing on the quantity of GM density. Furthermore, these maps are sensitive to subtle variations in the GM volume or concentration, which may occur in the early stages of AD manifestation, even before morphological changes are visible on linear-registered MRI scans. Thanks to such advantages, it can better depict brain atrophies, a hallmark of Alzheimer’s or other neurodegenerative diseases, making it widely used in medical image analysis as one of the quantitative features [34], [61], [62].

Nonetheless, exploiting the entire GM density maps alone might be inadequate for AD classification as it is hard to capture the subtle structural variations because of the aligning process. To overcome this drawback, we further utilized the ROI strategy to focus on specific regions where the GM density differences occur depending on the disease progression. In particular, since our AD-effect ROIs are only constructed via GM density values in highlighted regions that are quite sensitive to the variability of AD influence and highly related to AD manifestation, it is possible to boost the effectiveness of the ROI-based classification. To further verify the applicability of such in-depth analysis, an extensive evaluation was performed by utilizing other promising counterfactual-based approaches, as reported in Supplementary K.

Our predictive evaluation showed that LiCoL, despite being a linear classifier, outperformed all the comparative ML-based models considered in our study with substantial margins and was comparable to DL-based models. Under the linear property, We have further demonstrated that our LiCoL possesses a monotonicity similar to ML-based models, which are prone to comprehend the internal working. In particular, through the AD-relatedness index induced by the LiCoL’s inherent transparency, we could observe that each patient and group had a different contribution within ROIs, depending on the severity of morphological variations. By virtue of the LiCoL’s superiority, we thus claim that our method could be a stepping stone toward a comprehensible explanation of the deep models’ decisions and for predicting and analyzing neurodegenerative disease by leveraging quantitative figures.

5
CONCLUSION
In this work, we proposed a novel framework to analyze the counterfactual-induced visual explainability by transforming them into a GM density as a quantitative feature representation. Quantitative feature-based analysis using AD-effect ROIs helped conduct accurate numerical measurements based on the volumetric density changes in the brain caused by AD progression. Additionally, we designed a LiCoL, a simple shallow linear classifier, to boost the effectiveness of AD-effect ROIs while providing outstanding performance and the model’s interpretability. Under Li-CoL’s transparency, we further produced an AD-relatedness index that can be identified to intuitively understand the AD-related landmarks for an individual subject and groups.

We have viewed that utilizing visual explanation manipulated to quantitative figures is beneficial in yielding neuroscientific insights from a clinical aspect. However, there is still marginal room for improvement. Indeed, counterfactual reasoning regarding causality has to consider various confounders such as age, gender, or genetic factors, and the classification performance over multi-class scenarios must also be enhanced to provide more reliable interpretability. In this context, the future direction of this research would like to develop a model that adequately incorporates such demographic factors based on mutual relationships and derives outstanding performance in the multi-class scenarios while accounting for the nuanced differences among several disease stages via quantitative interpretation accordingly.

Heung-Il Suk’s affiliations include Gwangju, Republic of Korea, and the National Research Center for Dementia, Chosun University. His research is currently focused on brain image analysis and the creation of predictive models for neurodegenerative diseases. These models leverage both MRI data and genetic variants to improve understanding and potentially early detection of these conditions. This work represents a significant contribution to the field of neurological research, aiming to bridge the gap between imaging, genetics, and clinical application. The goal is to develop tools that can assist in diagnosis and potentially predict disease progression, ultimately improving patient care.

Dr. Suk received his foundational education in Computer Engineering, earning both a B.S. and M.S. from Pukyong National University in Busan, Korea, in 2004 and 2007, respectively. He continued his academic pursuits at Korea University in Seoul, South Korea, where he obtained his Ph.D. in Computer Science and Engineering in 2012. Following his doctoral studies, he undertook a Post-Doctoral Research Associate position at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill from 2012 to 2014, broadening his research experience in the United States.

Currently, Dr. Suk holds the position of Associate Professor within two departments at Korea University: the Department of Artificial Intelligence and the Department of Brain and Cognitive Engineering. His contributions have been recognized through prestigious awards, including a Kakao Faculty Fellowship from Kakao and a Young Researcher Award from the Korean Society for Human Brain Mapping (KHBM), received in 2018 and 2019, respectively. His research encompasses a wide range of areas, including machine/deep learning, explainable AI, biomedical data analysis, and brain-computer interface technologies.

Dr. Suk actively contributes to the scientific community through his service on editorial boards and participation in conference review processes. He is an Editorial Board Member for several prominent journals, including Electronics, Frontiers in Neuroscience, Frontiers in Radiology, International Journal of Imaging Systems and Technology (IJIST), and Clinical and Molecular Hepatology. Furthermore, he serves as a Program Committee member or Reviewer for numerous international conferences, such as NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI, IJCAI, CVPR, MICCAI, IPMI, and MIDL, demonstrating his commitment to advancing the field.
